feed.title: C, C++ & Rust — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Beej's Guides
entry.content:
Long-maintained, free and witty guides to C and network (socket) programming, offered as HTML, PDF and print. Unlike reference documentation they are written in a teaching voice.

https://beej.us/guide/

entry.title: Operation Costs in CPU Clock Cycles
entry.content:
The well-known infographic with explanation of the CPU clock-cycle cost of operations such as addition, memory access, branch mispredict and virtual calls. It gives orders of magnitude for performance intuition, not exact measurements.

https://6it.dev/blog/infographics-operation-costs-in-cpu-clock-cycles-741

entry.title: os-tutorial
entry.content:
A step-by-step tutorial that goes from a bootloader up to a kernel, one short folder per step. Shorter and more hands-on than books; it targets BIOS-based 32-bit x86. Maintenance is slow.

https://github.com/cfenollosa/os-tutorial

entry.title: The Little Book About OS Development
entry.content:
A free book on writing a simple x86 operating system from scratch: booting, memory, interrupts, system calls. Unlike large OS textbooks, it builds one small kernel from start to finish.

https://littleosbook.github.io/

entry.title: Write your Own Virtual Machine
entry.content:
A one-page tutorial on writing a virtual machine for the LC-3 architecture in C, ending with real LC-3 programs running. Unlike architecture lectures, it produces a working executor in a few hundred lines.

https://www.jmeiners.com/lc3-vm/

entry.title: cargo-binstall
entry.content:
A cargo plugin that installs Rust tools from prebuilt binaries instead of compiling. Unlike cargo install it takes seconds, not minutes.

https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall

entry.title: Awesome C++
entry.content:
A list organising C++ libraries and frameworks by topic. Unlike general search it is a maintained, categorised starting map.

https://github.com/uhub/awesome-cpp

entry.title: Awesome CMake
entry.content:
A list of scripts, modules and resources for CMake, the C/C++ build tool. Unlike the official docs, it picks guides to target-based “modern CMake” practice and ready-made modules.

https://github.com/onqtam/awesome-cmake

entry.title: Awesome Rust
entry.content:
A list organising Rust libraries and applications by topic. Unlike a crates.io search it is a curated, categorised and maintained starting map.

https://github.com/rust-unofficial/awesome-rust

entry.title: Rust by Example
entry.content:
The official resource giving each concept as a runnable, editable code example. Unlike the book it cuts the prose and leads with the example — for those who learn by trying.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/

entry.title: Rust Playground
entry.content:
The official space to compile and run Rust code in the browser with no install. Unlike a local setup it gives compiler output and ASM/MIR via a shareable link.

https://play.rust-lang.org/

entry.title: Rustlings
entry.content:
An exercise set teaching Rust by fixing small, broken snippets. Unlike reading-based resources it has you read and fix compiler errors by hand.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rustlings

entry.title: The Async Book
entry.content:
The official book on async/await and the Future model in Rust. Unlike general concurrency material it explains Rust’s distinctive, decoupled runtime approach.

https://rust-lang.github.io/async-book/

entry.title: The Cargo Book
entry.content:
The official guide to Cargo, Rust’s package manager and build tool. Unlike scattered blogs it gathers dependencies, workspaces and publishing in one authoritative place.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/

entry.title: The Rust Programming Language
entry.content:
Rust’s official book, building up ownership and borrowing from nothing. Unlike other language books it makes the compiler’s error messages part of the teaching — in Rust, learning to argue with the compiler is half the language.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/

entry.title: The Rust Reference
entry.content:
The official reference defining the language’s grammar and semantics. Unlike the book it is not a tutorial but the authoritative answer to “exactly how does Rust behave”.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/

entry.title: The Rustonomicon
entry.content:
An advanced book on the rules of unsafe Rust. Unlike the main book it covers what to watch for when you step outside the borrow checker.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/

entry.title: cppreference
entry.content:
The most widely used reference for the C and C++ standard library, marking which standard (C++11/17/20/23) each feature arrived in. Unlike tutorial sites, it never skips that version distinction.

https://cppreference.com/

entry.title: C++ Üslup ve Teknik SSS
entry.content:
Stroustrup’s FAQ on C++ style and common mistakes — direct answers to “why should I do it this way”. Unlike third-party tutorials, the reasoning comes from the language’s creator.

https://www.stroustrup.com/bs_faq2.html

entry.title: C++11 SSS (Stroustrup)
entry.content:
The language’s creator explaining why each C++11 feature was added. Unlike a feature list, it gives the design rationale.

https://www.stroustrup.com/C++11FAQ.html

entry.title: Comprehensive Rust
entry.content:
Google’s open four-day Rust course as slides + exercises. Unlike the book it is paced for a classroom and comes with embedded and concurrency modules.

https://google.github.io/comprehensive-rust/

entry.title: CppCon
entry.content:
Every talk from the annual C++ conference. Against tutorials it carries presentations from the people who write the standard — where you hear why a feature was designed as it was.

https://www.youtube.com/user/CppCon/videos?shelf_id=0&view=0&sort=dd

entry.title: crates.io
entry.content:
Rust’s official package registry — the hub for publishing libraries and pulling them as dependencies. Unlike general code search it shows the trustworthy source with version and download data.

https://crates.io/

entry.title: docs.rs
entry.content:
A service that automatically builds and publishes the docs for every package on crates.io. Unlike each project’s own site it gathers the whole ecosystem’s docs in one format at one address.

https://docs.rs/

entry.title: Meeting C++
entry.content:
The talk archive of one of Europe’s largest C++ conferences. Against CppCon it is smaller and more applied — experience from real projects rather than standards debate.

https://www.youtube.com/user/MeetingCPP/videos

entry.title: Qt Documentation
entry.content:
The official documentation for the Qt framework: class reference, examples and platform guides for C++ and QML. Against other UI framework docs the difference is scope — desktop, mobile and embedded described under one API.

https://doc.qt.io/

entry.title: Rust Cookbook
entry.content:
A cookbook of everyday tasks in Rust — read a file line by line, make an HTTP request. Against the book and the examples it is task-oriented: you open it to finish something, not to learn the language.

https://rust-lang-nursery.github.io/rust-cookbook/

entry.title: Rust Standard Library
entry.content:
The official reference for the Rust standard library — types, traits and macros. Unlike tutorials it aims not to teach but to be the complete, exact reference.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/

entry.title: Stroustrup on C++
entry.content:
The C++ creator’s own pages: FAQs, style advice and essays on why the language was designed as it was. Unlike tutorials it supplies rationale — the reason behind a decision is only available from the person who made it.

https://www.stroustrup.com/C++.html

entry.title: This Week in Rust
entry.content:
A newsletter rounding up developments, releases and posts in the Rust world weekly. Unlike scattered following it lets you track the ecosystem in one regular stream.

https://this-week-in-rust.org/

entry.title: Tokio
entry.content:
The most widely used asynchronous runtime for Rust; network services build on it. Unlike the standard library it brings a scheduler, tasks and tooling for highly concurrent I/O.

https://tokio.rs/

entry.title: Rust Öğrenin (Türkçe)
entry.content:
The Turkish version of Rust’s official learning page. Meeting ownership and borrowing in your own language rather than English softens the language’s steepest climb a little.

https://rust-lang.org/tr/learn/

entry.title: Learn C
entry.content:
A C tutorial you compile and run in the browser. Rather than installing a toolchain you try it on the page, which removes the entry barrier for anyone who wants a look at the language.

https://www.learn-c.org/

entry.title: C Programming Tutorial
entry.content:
A classic front-to-back treatment of C. Comprehensive, but dated in style and examples — handier for looking one topic up than for reading through.

https://www.tutorialspoint.com/cprogramming/index.htm

entry.title: C Yol Haritası
entry.content:
A short map ordering C topics. Unlike full courses it gives sequence rather than content, showing where pointers and memory management belong.

https://github.com/Koubae/Programming-CookBook/blob/master/Programming%20Languages/C/roadmap.md

entry.title: GeeksforGeeks C
entry.content:
C material split by topic. Unlike a sequential book, a search lands you straight on the relevant page; some examples rely on old compiler behaviour, so read carefully.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/c/c-programming-language/

entry.title: Awesome C
entry.content:
A list of C libraries, frameworks and tools. Because the standard library is deliberately thin, “which library” comes up far more often in C than elsewhere.

https://github.com/oz123/awesome-c

entry.title: IncludeHelp C Programları
entry.content:
A collection of solved C programs. Unlike tutorials it offers working examples instead of exposition — handy for recalling a pattern quickly.

https://www.includehelp.com/c-programs/c-programs-basic-input-output-operations.aspx

entry.title: Sıfırdan C Programlama
entry.content:
A Turkish video covering C in a single sitting. Unlike courses spread over weeks it is done in one go — for a fast introduction or pre-exam revision.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yuVatFCOISc

entry.title: Kodisyum C Örnekleri
entry.content:
Turkish C example programs covering the classic coursework-level exercises. Unlike English example archives it is in Turkish — valuable because Turkish C material is thin on the ground.

https://kodisyum.com/c-ornekler/
